lessons.title: A world inside a cell

blocks.text: Find the boundary
A plasma membrane separates a cell from its surroundings and controls exchange. Both a typical animal cell and a bacterium have one.
Where is the DNA?
In a eukaryotic cell, most DNA sits inside a membrane-bound nucleus. A bacterium has DNA in a nucleoid region, without that surrounding nuclear membrane. Its ribosomes make proteins.
Two energy jobs
Chloroplasts capture light energy in photosynthetic leaf cells. Mitochondria help transfer energy from fuel into ATP. Leaf cells have both.
Support outside
A plant cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and helps resist expansion. It does not replace the membrane's role in controlling exchange.

lessons.orientation: Connect cell structures to their jobs and distinguish bacteria from eukaryotes.

lessons.title: Which way will molecules move?

blocks.text: Follow the difference
Molecules move in both directions. If a membrane permits a solute to cross, unequal concentrations cause a net movement toward the less concentrated side.
Share the amount
With equal fixed volumes and a freely crossing solute, equilibrium has equal concentrations. The total amount of solute stays constant.
Check the gate
A concentration difference cannot move a substance through a barrier that blocks it. Permeability is part of the prediction.
Motion continues
Equal concentrations mean no net diffusion. Individual molecules still cross both ways at equal average rates.

lessons.orientation: Predict net diffusion from concentration and membrane permeability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: When only water can cross

blocks.text: Water follows a gradient
Osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane. With equal pressure, water initially moves toward the side with more concentrated impermeant solute.
Keep the solute
Water crosses this membrane but solute cannot. The solute amounts stay fixed while volumes change, so concentrations change.
Compare ratios
Concentration is amount divided by volume. Doubling water volume while keeping solute amount fixed halves the concentration.
Know the model's limit
The movable partition here allows volume change without building pressure. Real cell walls and pressure differences can oppose osmotic water movement.

lessons.orientation: Predict osmosis without confusing solute amount with concentration.

lessons.title: Make a reaction easier

blocks.text: Lower the barrier
Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy. They are regenerated during the reaction rather than used up as fuel.
Read a temperature curve
Temperature can increase reaction rate over one range and reduce it over another. High temperatures can disrupt an enzyme's shape; the best range depends on the enzyme.
A limited set of sites
With a fixed amount of enzyme, increasing substrate can eventually produce little extra rate. Many active sites are already occupied.
Change one cause
To test an enzyme's effect, compare otherwise matched conditions with and without it. Replication helps reveal how variable the measurements are.

lessons.orientation: Read enzyme data and distinguish catalysis, saturation and fair comparisons.

lessons.title: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

blocks.text: Build from air
In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide supplies the carbon used to build sugars. Light provides energy; it does not supply carbon atoms.
Count carbon
The simplified overall accounting is 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Six carbon dioxide molecules supply six carbon atoms for one glucose.
Follow the energy
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. Plants still need respiration to transfer energy from sugars into forms cells can use.
Find a limit
More light can raise photosynthetic rate over one range. A plateau suggests that extra light alone is no longer increasing rate under those conditions.

lessons.orientation: Trace carbon and energy through the overall photosynthesis reaction.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lessons.title: How does a cell use its fuel?

blocks.text: Transfer usable energy
During aerobic respiration, cells transfer some energy from fuel into ATP, while other energy disperses as heat. ATP can then drive cellular work.
Conserve carbon
For complete aerobic oxidation, one glucose gives six CO₂. Carbon atoms are rearranged into products rather than converted into energy.
Plants use fuel too
Plants respire in light and darkness. Photosynthesis needs light, but living plant cells still need ATP when light is absent.
Read a respiration signal
In a sealed measurement system with aerobic organisms, falling oxygen can indicate respiration. A matched blank helps separate organism activity from changes in the apparatus.

lessons.orientation: Connect respiration, ATP and conserved atoms without confusing breathing with cellular reactions.
lessons.reviewLabel: How does a cell use its fuel?

lessons.title: Copy a message one base at a time

blocks.text: Match a base
Complementary pairing makes each DNA strand a template. A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The strands run in opposite chemical directions.
Align the strands
When the top strand is read left to right as 5′-AAGC-3′, its aligned partner below reads 3′-TTCG-5′. These are opposite directions, not two parallel 5′-to-3′ readings.
Keep an old strand
DNA replication is semiconservative: each resulting double-stranded DNA molecule contains one old strand and one newly made strand.
Copies stay joined
After DNA replication, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined together. DNA amount has doubled, but chromosome number has not yet doubled.

lessons.orientation: Use complementary DNA bases and distinguish DNA amount from chromosome count.
lessons.reviewLabel: Copy a message one base at a time

lessons.title: Make two cells

blocks.text: A reason to divide
Cells divide for growth, repair and reproduction. Division is regulated; it is not simply a response to being about to die.
Prepare a copy
Before mitosis, DNA is replicated. Each chromosome then has two sister chromatids, ready to be separated into the daughter nuclei.
Share the copies
During mitosis, sister chromatids separate. After division and cytokinesis, the two daughter cells normally retain the starting chromosome number.
Repeat with care
In an ideal sequence where every cell divides once per round, cell number doubles each round. Real tissues regulate which cells divide and when.

lessons.orientation: Track chromosomes through mitotic division and connect division to growth and repair.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Halve a chromosome set

blocks.text: Pairs and sets
A diploid cell has two chromosome sets. Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding genes, though they may carry different alleles. Meiosis reduces two sets to one.
Separate homologues
In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes separate. At its end, each daughter has one chromosome from each pair, still made of joined sister chromatids.
Separate sisters
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids without another preceding DNA replication. The simplified model ends with four haploid cells.
Restore two sets
At fertilisation, two haploid chromosome sets combine. This restores diploidy. Crossing over and chromosome assortment also make sexual offspring genetically varied.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish homologues from sister chromatids and follow two meiotic divisions.

lessons.title: What could the offspring inherit?

blocks.text: One allele per gamete
In this diploid single-gene model, an Aa parent forms A and a gametes with equal probability. Each offspring receives one allele from each parent.
Four equal pairings
Crossing Aa with Aa gives four equally likely pairings: AA, Aa, Aa and aa. The repeated Aa squares represent separate ways to get that genotype.
A trait is not a genotype
With complete dominance, AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype. The recessive phenotype requires aa in this model.
Chances are not quotas
A 25% probability applies to each independent offspring. Four offspring need not include exactly one recessive individual.

lessons.orientation: Use a single-gene cross while separating genotype, phenotype and probability.

lessons.title: Where does a new variant come from?

blocks.text: Change the sequence
A mutation changes DNA sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another; insertions and deletions add or remove bases.
Count the change
Two sequences can differ at a single position without changing length. Sequence change alone does not tell you whether a biological effect is harmful, neutral or helpful.
Pass it onward
In sexually reproducing animals, a mutation in the cell lineage that forms gametes can reach offspring. A mutation confined to an ordinary body cell generally does not.
Variation before selection
Mutations do not arise because an organism needs a particular useful change. Selection acts on existing heritable differences; its outcome depends on the environment.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish DNA change from directed need and identify what can be inherited.
lessons.reviewLabel: Where does a new variant come from?

lessons.title: A population changes over generations

blocks.text: Count a frequency
Frequency is a fraction of a population. If 10 of 40 organisms carry the blue variant, its frequency is 25%. Counts and proportions answer different questions.
Follow descendants
Natural selection requires heritable differences associated with different reproductive success. A helpful trait in one environment need not help in another.
Populations evolve
Selection changes a population's composition over generations. It does not mean an individual develops a needed inherited trait during its own lifetime.
Keep alternative causes
A frequency shift alone does not prove selection. Chance sampling, migration and other processes can also alter a population's composition.

lessons.orientation: Connect heritable variation and reproductive success without confusing change with proof of cause.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Follow the food

blocks.text: Read the arrow
A feeding arrow points from food to the organism consuming it. Grass → grasshopper means the grasshopper obtains matter and energy from grass.
Find the producers
Primary producers build organic matter using an external energy source. Grass and algae in these webs capture light through photosynthesis.
More than one route
A food web can contain several routes to the same consumer. In the meadow, energy can reach a hawk through mice or through grasshoppers and frogs.
Recycle matter
Decomposers return matter from dead material to environmental pools. Energy disperses as heat through ecosystem processes and needs continuing input; it is not recycled like atoms.

lessons.orientation: Read feeding arrows and separate energy flow from recycled matter.

lessons.title: Why does less energy reach the top?

blocks.text: A fraction is transferred
Only some production at one trophic level becomes production at the next. Organisms use energy in metabolism, and not all material is eaten or assimilated.
Apply it twice
A transfer percentage applies at each step. Two 10% transfers leave 1% of the initial energy at the third level.
Compare efficiencies
Transfer efficiency varies between systems. A stated 20% is a problem assumption, not a universal law. On the same initial energy, it transfers more than 10%.
Work backward
To support a target amount at a consumer level, divide by the assumed transfer fraction to find the required energy at the level below.

lessons.orientation: Calculate trophic transfers using an explicit efficiency assumption.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why does less energy reach the top?

lessons.title: Why can't a population grow forever?

blocks.text: Growth can multiply
Under ideal conditions, a constant proportional growth rate makes increases larger as population size grows. Repeated doubling is one example.
Resources set limits
As resources become scarce, competition can reduce births or increase deaths. In a simple logistic model, net growth approaches zero near carrying capacity.
Balance the rates
A stable population size can hide ongoing births and deaths. Zero net growth means gains and losses balance, not that every organism stops reproducing.
Capacity can change
Carrying capacity depends on conditions. A drought or habitat loss can reduce the population that the environment supports; it is not a permanent species constant.

lessons.orientation: Compare proportional growth with resource-limited growth and changing carrying capacity.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why can't a population grow forever?

lessons.title: What would count as evidence?

blocks.text: Ask a testable question
A claim about fertiliser and plant growth can be tested by measuring growth in comparable treated and untreated plants. Define the outcome before measuring it.
Subtract a baseline
If groups start at different heights, final height alone can mislead. Compare change from baseline and consider whether groups were comparable before treatment.
Replicate and assign
Random assignment reduces systematic differences between treatment groups. Independent replicates help estimate variability; repeatedly measuring one pot is not the same as using many pots.
Leave room for causes
An observational association can suggest a hypothesis, but does not by itself isolate a cause. Other environmental factors may explain the pattern.

lessons.orientation: Design fair ecological comparisons and avoid turning correlation into an unsupported cause.

questions.prompt: Name the boundary that controls exchange in both illustrated animal and bacterial cells.
hints: Inspect the boundary around each cell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both cells exchange substances across a plasma membrane.

questions.prompt: The bacterium has no membrane-bound nucleus. Where is its DNA?

questions.prompt: Which pair can occur together in the illustrated photosynthetic leaf cell?

questions.prompt: Name the supporting structure outside the plant cell membrane.
hints: Inspect the outermost layer of the leaf cell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cell wall provides external support; the membrane remains inside it.

questions.prompt: A root cell is alive but has no chloroplasts. Which conclusion follows?
hints: Consider the cell's location and job.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many plant cells, including many root cells, lack chloroplasts and use sugars supplied by other tissues.

choices.label: It cannot be a plant cell
It cannot release energy from fuel

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly identifies a cell as eukaryotic?
hints: Choose the distinctive structure, not a shared feature.

acceptedIdeas: DNA enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A membrane-bound nucleus distinguishes eukaryotic organisation from bacterial organisation.

choices.label: DNA enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus

questions.prompt: Equal volumes contain 12 solute units on the left and 4 on the right. Solute can cross. What is the initial net direction?
hints: Compare amounts only because the volumes are equal.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The concentration is initially higher on the left, so net solute movement is to the right.

questions.prompt: Two fixed equal volumes contain 10 and 6 units of freely crossing solute. How many units are on each side at equilibrium?
hints: Keep the total solute constant.
Add 10 and 6.
Divide the total between two equal volumes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 16 units divide equally: 16/2 = 8.

questions.prompt: The barrier blocks both solute and water. What happens to the initial 12:4 solute amounts?
hints: Check permeability before following a gradient.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Neither substance can cross this barrier, so the amounts stay as given.

questions.prompt: At equal concentration, 8 units are on each side. How many solute units are in the whole two-compartment system?
hints: Count both compartments.
There are eight units in each.
Add the two equal amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 + 8 = 16 units; diffusion does not destroy solute.

questions.prompt: At diffusion equilibrium, which statement is accurate?
hints: Distinguish no net change from no motion.

acceptedIdeas: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equilibrium is dynamic: opposite flows balance on average.

choices.label: Molecules cross both ways with no net flow
All molecules move in one direction

questions.prompt: A separate equal-volume system starts with 14 solute units on one side and 2 on the other. How many units must move net from the concentrated side to reach equilibrium?
hints: Find the equilibrium amount first.
The total is 16 across two equal volumes.
Subtract the equilibrium amount from 14.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each side finishes with 8. The concentrated side loses 14 − 8 = 6.

questions.prompt: Water can cross but solute cannot. Equal volumes contain 4 solute units left and 12 right at equal pressure. Name the side that initially gains water.
hints: Compare concentration, then follow water.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right side has the higher impermeant-solute concentration and initially gains water.

questions.prompt: As water enters the right compartment, what happens to its 12 solute units?
hints: The membrane's selectivity stays the same.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The membrane blocks solute; only its concentration changes.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 12 solute units in volume 2. What is its concentration in units per volume?
hints: Use amount divided by volume.
The amount is 12 and volume is 2.
Divide 12 by 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration = 12/2 = 6 units per volume.

questions.prompt: Why can the model's two volumes change while its total solute remains constant?
hints: Follow each substance separately.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing water distribution changes volumes without changing solute amount.

questions.prompt: A compartment contains 8 units of trapped solute. Its volume increases from 1 to 2. By what factor is its concentration multiplied?
hints: Calculate concentration before and after.
The solute amount is unchanged.
Divide the new concentration by the old one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Concentration changes from 8 to 4, a factor of 4/8 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: A plant cell wall builds an opposing pressure as water enters. Which prediction is justified?
hints: The real cell includes a force missing from the model.

acceptedIdeas: Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water movement depends on both solute concentration and pressure; the simple partition model omits this opposition.

choices.label: Water must keep entering without limit
Pressure can reduce or stop net water entry

Read rate on the vertical axis.
Use the plotted value, not a universal optimum.

hints: Ask which component supplies active sites.

hints: Compare the same elapsed time.
Read both values at three minutes.

hints: A protein's shape matters to its function.

choices.label: Every enzyme works best at that temperature

hints: Separate the tested factor from other possible causes.

acceptedIdeas: Compare matched replicated samples differing only in enzyme addition

Compare matched replicated samples differing only in enzyme addition
Compare different organisms at unrelated times

questions.prompt: Name the gas that supplies carbon atoms for newly made sugars during photosynthesis.
hints: Trace atoms separately from energy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon atoms; light supplies energy.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?
hints: Count carbon in both glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms.
Each CO₂ contributes one carbon atom.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two glucose contain 12 carbon atoms, requiring 12 CO₂.

questions.prompt: What happens to energy in photosynthesis?
hints: Keep matter and energy separate.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Photosynthetic reactions capture some incoming light energy in chemical form.

questions.prompt: On the lower-CO₂ curve, rate is 8 at both light levels 60 and 80. What is the measured rate increase?
hints: Use the lower-CO₂ curve.
Read the two rates at 60 and 80.
Subtract the first rate from the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 8 = 0; this interval is a plateau.

questions.prompt: A leaf cell has chloroplasts. What else may it do?
hints: Photosynthesis does not replace every other cell process.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells also respire to support their energy needs.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified overall equation, how many O₂ molecules accompany the formation of three glucose molecules?
hints: Read the coefficient beside O₂.
Use six oxygen molecules per glucose.
Multiply by three glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose corresponds to six O₂: 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.prompt: Name the molecule that commonly transfers energy from respiration to cellular work.
hints: The molecule has three phosphate groups.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP couples energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.

questions.prompt: Complete aerobic oxidation of two glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?
hints: Each CO₂ contains one carbon.
Each glucose contains six carbons.
Count the carbon from two glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.prompt: A living plant has stored fuel and oxygen but no light. Name the energy-transfer process that can continue.
hints: Which process uses fuel rather than requiring incoming light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Respiration can use stored fuel in darkness even when photosynthesis stops.

questions.prompt: In the organisms case, oxygen falls from 20 to 11 units in three minutes. How many units were consumed?
hints: Compare the initial and final oxygen amounts.
The final amount is lower.
Subtract 11 from 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 − 11 = 9 oxygen units.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon during complete aerobic oxidation?
hints: Follow carbon-containing substances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly distinguishes breathing and respiration?
hints: Compare movement of air with cellular chemistry.

Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions

hints: DNA amount and chromosome number are different counts.
Joined sister chromatids belong to one replicated chromosome.
Keep the chromosome count unchanged at this stage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It still has four chromosomes; each now has two sister chromatids.

questions.prompt: What does semiconservative replication conserve in each resulting DNA molecule?
hints: Trace the two original strands separately.

questions.prompt: Six chromosomes each have two sister chromatids after copying. How many DNA molecules are present?
hints: Count both chromatids of each chromosome.
There are six replicated chromosomes.
Multiply six by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each chromatid contains one DNA molecule: 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.prompt: Name the nuclear division process used in ordinary tissue growth and repair.
hints: It preserves the starting chromosome number.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mitosis distributes copied chromosomes to daughter nuclei during regulated growth and repair.

questions.prompt: A cell has 6 chromosomes before replication. How many DNA molecules does it have after replication but before mitosis?
hints: Replication copies the DNA.
Each of six chromosomes has two chromatids.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six replicated chromosomes have two chromatids each: 12 DNA molecules.

questions.prompt: A cell starts with 4 chromosomes and completes normal mitosis and cytokinesis. How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
hints: Track copies delivered to one daughter.
Sister chromatids are separated equally.
Mitosis preserves this starting chromosome number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each daughter retains the original four chromosomes.

questions.prompt: One cell completes three ideal rounds of division, with every descendant dividing each round. How many cells result?
hints: Double once for each round.
After two rounds there are four cells.
Double the count a third time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.

questions.prompt: Name the two joined copies of a replicated chromosome that separate during mitosis.
hints: Track the two copies made by DNA replication.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sister chromatids separate and become daughter chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Does a normal body cell divide only because it is about to die?
hints: Separate regulated division from cell death.

acceptedIdeas: No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cell-cycle regulation responds to conditions and signals; imminent death is not the general cause.

No, division is regulated for growth, repair and other needs
Yes, and DNA need not be copied

questions.prompt: A diploid cell has 3 homologous pairs. How many chromosomes does it contain before DNA replication?
hints: Each pair contains two homologues.
There are three pairs.
Multiply three by two.

questions.prompt: Which chromosome relationship is separated during meiosis I: name the paired chromosomes.
hints: The pair contains corresponding chromosomes from the two sets.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate first; sister chromatids remain joined.

questions.prompt: A starting cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. After the two meiotic divisions, how many chromosomes does each final cell have?
hints: Meiosis reduces two chromosome sets to one.
The starting cell has two homologous pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each final haploid cell has one from each pair: two chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Two gametes each contain 3 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in their diploid fertilisation product?
hints: Fertilisation combines the two sets.
Each gamete supplies three chromosomes.
Add the two contributions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 + 3 = 6 chromosomes.

questions.prompt: How many additional DNA-replication rounds normally occur between meiosis I and meiosis II?
hints: Trace the copied chromosomes through both divisions.
Meiosis begins with one replication round.
The DNA is divided again without being recopied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No additional replication occurs; the second division separates existing sister chromatids.

questions.prompt: Why can siblings inherit different chromosome combinations?
hints: Chromosome counts can match while genetic combinations differ.

acceptedIdeas: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Assortment and crossing over produce varied gametes; the simple count diagram omits crossover.

choices.label: Chromosomes assort and exchange segments during meiosis
Each parent has no genetic variation

questions.prompt: What term describes the Aa parent, which carries two different alleles at this locus?
hints: The term contrasts with homozygous.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aa is heterozygous; its two different alleles can segregate into gametes.

questions.prompt: For Aa × Aa, what percentage of offspring is expected to have genotype aa?
hints: Inspect all four pairings.
Count the aa squares.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One of four equally likely pairings is aa: 1/4 = 25%.

questions.prompt: With A completely dominant, which genotypes have the dominant phenotype?
hints: Keep genotype letters separate from the expressed trait.

acceptedIdeas: Two dominant alleles or one of each
